坐或站，將鼓置於身前合適位置。將鼓穩定放置於地面或夾於雙腿之間。用手掌或鼓棒敲擊: Sit or stand and put the drum in a suitable position in front of you. Set the drum firmly on the ground or hold it between the legs. Strike the centre or the edge of the head with the palm or a stick; different positions give different tones. The force of the stroke sets the volume. The sound is made by striking, so watch the position and the force.
阿希科傳統以硬木製成，鼓面多用小牛皮，現代有時用山羊皮以模仿金貝鼓高音。傳統鼓身: The ashiko is traditionally made of hardwood, and the head is mostly calfskin; today goatskin is sometimes used to imitate the high pitch of the djembe. The traditional body is carved by hand from a single log and is not a straight cone but curved inside. Western modern products often join straight wooden staves, can be tuned with rope, and also come with metal bolts and metal pins; some use cowhide. The materials of the other parts are not stated in the sources.

阿希科錐形鼓傳統上出現在約魯巴文化的社區慶祝與說話鼓場合，也見於非裔加勒比與非裔: The ashiko traditionally appears at Yoruba community celebrations and in talking-drum settings, and also in Afro-Caribbean and Afro-Latin traditions: the "bocú" of eastern Cuba, the solo drum of the Abakuá secret society, and the "Tambor Alegre" of the Colombian Caribbean. The "timbau" of Bahia in Brazil is of a similar form. In the United States it was heard through Babatunde Olatunji's folk ensemble and the albums Drums of Passion and More Drums of Passion, and it entered local drum circles in Europe and America.
阿希科錐形鼓起源於西非約魯巴文化，主要在今奈及利亞與貝南一帶，傳統上用於社群慶典: The ashiko comes from Yoruba culture in West Africa, mainly in what is now Nigeria and Benin, and was traditionally used for community celebrations and as a talking drum. Early instruments were hollowed by hand from a whole piece of hardwood, not a straight cone. After the slave trade, similar drum forms appear in Afro-Caribbean and Latin American traditions. In the 1930s the Nigerian drummer Moses Mians moved to New York and the drum began to spread in the United States; in the 1950s and 1960s Babatunde Olatunji's touring folk ensemble widened its influence, and after the 1980s it entered European and American drum circles, though interest has since fallen off.
阿希科錐形鼓（Ashiko）屬膜鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號: The ashiko (Ashiko) is a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.251.1, a truncated cone drum with skin on the wide end and open at the narrow end. It is traditionally of hardwood, the head mostly calfskin and later also goatskin, to imitate the high pitch of the djembe. It is played by hand and tuned with rope. Its origin goes back to Yoruba culture in West Africa, mainly in what is now Nigeria and Benin, where it was traditionally used for community celebrations and also served as a talking drum.
阿希科鼓音色深沉而富有共鳴，具有溫潤的暗沉質感，帶有明顯的非洲鼓樂特色。其音域偏: The ashiko's timbre is deep and resonant, with a warm, dark quality and an obvious African percussion character. Its range is low to low-middle: struck on the wide head it gives a full, thick low boom, and nearer the narrow end it gives a brighter middle note. The conical structure makes the sound wave resonate in a particular way inside, so the tone carries and rings well. Against the sharp high djembe the ashiko sounds heavier and fuller; against drums with a strong metallic edge it has a warmer, more organic quality. Its tone can drive a powerful groove and can also build a deep, soulful mood, which makes it a natural instrument for fusing African tradition with modern music.
